# Glossary {.unnumbered}

Every term this book sets in bold is defined here, written to be read cold by
somebody who doesn't have the chapter open. The chapter named at the end of
each entry is where the term gets taught with a worked example. Error messages
are not in this list. Those are in the error index, which gives you a page
number for each one.

## A {.unnumbered}

**accession number**
: A permanent identifier for one record in a sequence database, such as
  `NM_007294.4`. The part after the dot is the version, and it goes up each
  time somebody corrects the sequence. Quote an accession without its version
  and you've named a record that can change under you. See Chapter 5.

**affine gap penalty**
: A way of pricing gaps in an alignment that charges a large amount to open a
  gap and a small amount for each further column the gap runs on. One deletion
  of twelve bases is a single event, and this pricing is what stops a program
  from scoring it like twelve separate one-base events. See Chapter 18.

## B {.unnumbered}

**BED**
: A tab-separated text format for intervals along a sequence, with three
  required columns: the sequence name, the start, and the end. Coordinates
  count from zero and the end position is not included, which is the opposite
  convention from GenBank and GFF. See Chapter 15.

**bioinformatics**
: Building and running the software and the databases that hold biological
  data and hand it back to whoever asks. BLAST is bioinformatics, and so is
  the collection of sequences it searches. See Chapter 2.

**bit score**
: An alignment score put on a fixed scale, so the same value means the same
  thing in every search anyone has ever run. Unlike an E-value it doesn't move
  when the database changes size, which is why it's the column you compare
  hits across searches with. See Chapter 7.

**BLAST**
: Basic Local Alignment Search Tool. You hand it one sequence, and it hands
  back the deposited sequences that resemble yours region by region, ranked
  and scored. See Chapter 6.

## C {.unnumbered}

**cell**
: One box in a notebook, holding either code or text. They run one at a time
  in whatever order you click, so a notebook can show a result that no
  top-to-bottom run reproduces. See Chapter 4.

**computational biology**
: Using computation to answer a question about biology rather than to build a
  tool. The output is an answer, such as which two species split first. See
  Chapter 2.

**counts per million**
: A raw count divided by the total counts in its own sample, then multiplied
  by a million. It makes one gene comparable across samples sequenced to
  different depths. A count is still not an amount of RNA, because it mixes
  how much the cell held with how hard the machine looked. See Chapter 20.

## D {.unnumbered}

**DataFrame**
: A table in pandas, with named columns, numbered rows, and one kind of value
  all the way down each column. It's what you get back when you read a
  spreadsheet or a counts file into Python. See Chapter 20.

**dictionary**
: A set of key and value pairs, where you fetch a value by naming its key
  instead of by its position. A key appears once, so asking for a key that
  isn't there raises `KeyError` rather than giving you an empty answer. See
  Chapter 13.

**differential expression**
: Comparing one gene's counts between two groups of samples, then repeating
  that comparison for every gene in the table. What gets compared are
  normalized counts and never expression itself. A count measures the
  sequencing run as much as it measures the cell. See Chapter 24.

**docstring**
: A string written on the first line of a function's body, in triple quotes,
  saying what the function does and what it assumes about its input. Python
  keeps it, instead of throwing it away the way it throws away a comment. See
  Chapter 14.

**domain**
: A stretch of a protein that folds up on its own and does its own job, even
  when it's cut out of the full chain. Domains carry names and the residue
  numbers they run between, which is how a database annotates them. See
  Chapter 8.

## E {.unnumbered}

**Entrez Gene ID**
: NCBI's permanent integer identifier for one gene in one species. It never
  changes and never comes to point at another gene. It also tells you nothing
  on sight, so a table of them needs a lookup before you can read it. See
  Chapter 20.

**E-value**
: The number of alignments at least this good that you'd expect to meet by
  accident in a database this size. It counts expected accidents, which is
  neither the probability that your hit is real nor a p-value. Search a bigger
  database and the same alignment earns a bigger E-value. See Chapter 7.

## F {.unnumbered}

**false discovery rate**
: The expected fraction of the hits on your list that are false positives. Set
  it to 0.05 and you accept one wrong gene in twenty on the list you report.
  That's a different promise from a p-value cutoff of 0.05. See Chapter 25.

**FASTA**
: A plain-text sequence format: one header line starting with a greater-than
  sign, then the sequence on the lines after it. Nothing in the format says
  which organism the sequence came from or whether it's DNA or protein. All of
  that lives in the header, and the header is free text. See Chapter 5.

**FASTQ**
: FASTA with a confidence attached to every base. Four lines make one read: a
  name line starting with an at sign, the bases, a plus line, then one quality
  character per base. Line four is always the same length as line two. See
  Chapter 15.

**function**
: A block of code with a name, which you run by writing the name and a pair of
  brackets. The body doesn't run when Python reads it; it runs when something
  calls the name. See Chapter 14.

## G {.unnumbered}

**GenBank flatfile**
: NCBI's full text record for one sequence: a description, the papers behind
  it, annotated features with their coordinates, then the sequence itself.
  It's what you get when nothing is left out. The FASTA version of the same
  record throws all of it away except the sequence. See Chapter 15.

**genome assembly**
: One numbered reconstruction of a genome, such as GRCh37 or GRCh38. A
  coordinate means nothing without the name of the assembly it was counted in.
  Sequence gets added and reordered between assemblies, so every position
  downstream of a change moves. See Chapter 5.

**global alignment**
: An alignment forced to run end to end through both sequences, with every
  base in both pushed into some column. Ask for one when you expect the whole
  of both sequences to correspond, and a local alignment when you don't. See
  Chapter 18.

**guide tree**
: A rough tree that an alignment program builds for itself, to decide what
  order to align the sequences in. It's a scheduling device, and it makes no
  claim about history. Keep it apart from the tree the program hands you when
  the run finishes. See Chapter 19.

## H {.unnumbered}

**heatmap**
: A table drawn as colored squares, one square per cell of the table, so the
  pattern across rows and columns shows at a glance. In an expression figure
  it's one row per gene and one column per sample, so every sample stays
  visible instead of being summarized away. See Chapter 21.

**homologous**
: Descended from a common ancestor. That's a claim about history, and it's
  either true or false. Nothing is 60 percent homologous, and what a paper
  calls percent homology is really percent identity. See Chapter 7.

## I {.unnumbered}

**indel**
: An insertion or a deletion, at a place where two aligned sequences disagree
  by a gap. Which one it is depends on which sequence you treat as the
  original, and an alignment can't tell you that. See Chapter 18.

**issues**
: The numbered public threads on a code project's tracker, where somebody
  reports a problem and the maintainers answer. Anybody with a free account
  can open one and nobody assigns them, so reading a few is the cheapest way
  to see how a project really works. See Chapter 28.

## L {.unnumbered}

**library**
: Code somebody else wrote and published for other people to call. You install
  it once, import it by name, then use the names inside it as if you'd written
  them yourself. See Chapter 17.

**library size**
: The total number of reads counted in one sample, which is the sum of that
  sample's column in a counts table. Two samples with different library sizes
  can't have their raw counts compared directly. Counts per million exist to
  fix exactly that. See Chapter 20.

**list**
: An ordered run of values in Python, written inside square brackets. You
  reach a value by its position, counting from zero, so the first item sits at
  position 0. See Chapter 13.

**local alignment**
: An alignment that reports only the best-scoring stretch and is free to
  ignore the rest of both sequences. BLAST is local, which is why a hit can
  cover a small piece of your query and still score well. See Chapter 18.

## M {.unnumbered}

**MANE Select**
: The one transcript per human gene that NCBI and EMBL-EBI went through and
  agreed is representative, matching between their two databases. Use it when
  you need one human transcript and have no specific reason to want another.
  MANE covers human and not mouse. See Chapter 5.

**marker gene**
: A gene whose expression is reliably high in one cell type and low in
  another, used to tell those cell types apart. Checking one in your own table
  is how you find out whether the sample labels are the right way round. See
  Chapter 24.

**minimal reproducible example**
: The smallest piece of code that still produces your error, with everything
  unrelated cut away. Every line you delete is a line you've ruled out, so the
  cutting is the same work as finding the bug and sometimes finishes it. See
  Chapter 16.

**multiple sequence alignment**
: One alignment of three or more sequences, in which every column makes a
  single claim about all of them at once. A pair that would rather have its
  gap three bases along doesn't get it, because the column has to hold for
  every pair in the set. See Chapter 19.

## N {.unnumbered}

**Newick**
: A text format for trees. Parentheses group, commas separate, a colon and a
  number give a branch length, and a semicolon ends the tree. See Chapter 19.

## O {.unnumbered}

**outgroup**
: A sequence you add to a tree on purpose, chosen because you're already sure
  it sits outside the group you're studying. The branch leading to it is where
  the root goes, and every other branch takes its direction from that. See
  Chapter 19.

## P {.unnumbered}

**pairwise alignment**
: Two sequences written one above the other with gaps allowed in either, so
  every column holds one base from each or a base against a gap. The format
  has no other rules, and the scoring is what picks one arrangement out of the
  many possible ones. See Chapter 18.

**parameter**
: The name a function gives to a value it was handed. It exists only while the
  function is running, and it has nothing to do with the name that value had
  outside. See Chapter 14.

**percent identity**
: The share of alignment columns where both sequences carry the same base or
  residue. The denominator is a choice that varies between programs, so two
  tools can report different percent identities for one alignment. Don't read
  it as homology, which is a claim about ancestry rather than a measurement.
  See Chapter 18.

**Phred quality score**
: A number saying how likely the machine thinks a base call is wrong. Q20 is
  one error in a hundred and Q30 is one in a thousand, so every 10 points is a
  factor of ten in the error rate. See Chapter 15.

**pLDDT**
: AlphaFold's confidence in its own prediction at one residue, on a scale of 0
  to 100. High means the model is sure of the local shape there. No experiment
  enters into the number, so a confident model is still a prediction. See
  Chapter 8.

**principal component analysis**
: A way of redrawing many measurements per sample as two, chosen so that
  samples far apart in the full table stay far apart in the drawing. It also
  reports what fraction of the total spread each of the two directions holds.
  See Chapter 21.

**p-value**
: The chance of seeing a difference at least this big between two groups when
  there's no real difference at all. It knows nothing about how many other
  tests you ran, which is why a table of thousands of them needs a false
  discovery rate on top. An E-value is a different quantity and isn't a
  probability at all. See Chapter 25.

## Q {.unnumbered}

**query coverage**
: The percentage of your query sequence that the reported alignment actually
  covered. Read it next to percent identity and never alone: a hit can be 100
  percent identical over 28 bases of a long query and mean nothing. See
  Chapter 7.

## R {.unnumbered}

**reading frame**
: Which of the three ways of chopping a sequence into triplets you're using.
  Shift the start by one base and every codon after it changes, so only one of
  the three frames produces the protein. See Chapter 12.

**repository**
: One project's folder on a code-hosting site, with a web address of its own
  and a record of every change made to it. A public one on GitHub costs
  nothing, and it's where the work you want a hiring manager to see should
  live. See Chapter 26.

**runtime**
: The remote machine that runs the cells of your notebook. It holds every
  variable you have made, it's separate from the page in front of you, and it
  can die while the page still looks healthy. See Chapter 4.

## S {.unnumbered}

**script**
: A list of instructions saved in a file, so a machine can run the same steps
  again without you retyping them. That's the whole definition, and it's
  smaller than the word sounds. See Chapter 10.

**Seq**
: Biopython's sequence object. It slices and counts like an ordinary Python
  string, and it also knows how to complement and translate itself. See
  Chapter 17.

**SeqRecord**
: Biopython's object for one record read out of a sequence file: an id, a
  description, and the sequence itself. The id stops at the first space and
  the description keeps everything after it. Two records whose headers agree
  up to the first space therefore end up with the same id. See Chapter 17.

**slice**
: A run of characters cut out of a string, written `name[start:end]`. The end
  number is a gap rather than a letter, so that last letter isn't included and
  the length is end minus start. See Chapter 11.

**start codon**
: The ATG where translation begins. The same three letters appear all over a
  gene and code methionine in those places. Position is what makes one a start
  codon, because the ribosome loads on the front of the messenger RNA and
  begins at the first ATG it meets. See Chapter 12.

**string**
: An ordered run of characters that a program keeps as one value. The order is
  remembered exactly and the meaning is not remembered at all, because there's
  nowhere in a string to record what the characters stand for. See Chapter 11.

**substitution matrix**
: A table giving a score for every pair of amino acids, built by counting how
  often each swap turns up in alignments of sequences already known to be
  related. Protein alignment needs one because the twenty residues aren't
  interchangeable. DNA gets by with a single match score and a single mismatch
  score. See Chapter 18.

**systems biology**
: The study of how genes and proteins behave in groups, rather than one gene
  at a time. A network can do things you can't recover from any single member
  of it. See Chapter 2.

## T {.unnumbered}

**traceback**
: The block Python prints when it stops: a list of the lines it was inside,
  innermost last, then the error. Read the last line first, because that's the
  one sentence in the block written for a person. See Chapter 16.

**transcripts**
: The RNA versions of a gene, differing from each other in which exons they
  include. A gene is not a transcript. One gene has a single Gene record and
  many transcript records, so a gene length and a transcript length are
  different numbers. See Chapter 5.

## V {.unnumbered}

**variable**
: A name attached to a value, so the value can be used again by name. Nothing
  is copied and nothing is stored twice, because what you have made is a
  label. See Chapter 11.

**VCF**
: Variant Call Format. One line per position where a sample differs from a
  named reference genome, carrying the reference base and the alternate base,
  and nothing else. See Chapter 15.

**volcano plot**
: A scatter plot with one point per gene, showing how far the gene moved
  across the bottom and how well the move is supported up the side. It exists
  so you never have to choose between fold change and p-value. Sorting by
  either one alone gives you a list you would regret. See Chapter 21.
